idiom_name: method composed of unexported (lower-case) method calls
implementation_notes: Go methods are declared on a named type, and a body that only calls other methods of the same receiver is idiomatic; step methods are lower-case so they are unexported and therefore invisible outside the package, which is Go's encapsulation boundary. Effective Go's push for small functions and explicit error returns makes the style native, though the repeated if err != nil after each call means Go authors often stop decomposing earlier than authors in languages with exceptions.
pitfalls: Unexported means package-private, not type-private: any file in the same package can call c.reserveStock(), so the step is not a hard boundary.

Every step that can fail adds three lines of error handling to the coordinator; without wrapping (fmt.Errorf("charge: %w", err)) the sequence loses its context, and with it the coordinator drowns in plumbing.
A step promoted to an exported name changes the type's exported API and can silently change the interfaces the type satisfies; keep steps unexported and specifically named.
